note: Reference sample toolkits written to the app's exact format and rules (5-8 tools with theory, steps, what to say and a case study; 5 scenario quiz questions; a coached practice scenario). Use as a quality benchmark for generated bites.

samples.heading: Influence, Negotiation and Sales
learner: Main goal: Communicate and influence with impact

bite.title: Be the calmest, clearest person in the room
bite.framework: The Weight–Warmth–Focus model: six tools to show judgment under pressure, signal you're on their side, and hold attention when it counts. Use the first three to prepare, the last three in the moment.

tools.name: Answer First
tools.idea: Senior audiences judge in minutes. Lead with your conclusion or recommendation, then give the few reasons that support it. Starting with background makes you sound unsure; starting with the answer signals command. It also lets busy leaders decide quickly whether they need more detail.
steps: Write your recommendation in one sentence before the meeting.
Pick the three strongest reasons, no more.
Open with the answer; offer detail only when asked.
say: My recommendation is to pause phase two for six weeks. Three reasons.
Short answer: yes, with one condition. Let me explain the condition.

caseStudy.situation: A consulting partner had ten minutes with a client CEO to win approval for a revised programme budget.
caseStudy.action: She opened: “I'm asking you to approve a 12% budget increase today, because it brings go-live forward by a quarter.” Then she gave three reasons and stopped talking.
caseStudy.result: The CEO approved it in eight minutes and asked her to present to the board.

tools.tryThis: Rewrite the opening of your next update so the first sentence is your recommendation.

tools.name: Calm Under Fire
tools.idea: Gravitas shows most when things go wrong. Leaders who stay composed, own the problem and move to next steps are trusted more than those who defend or deflect. Acknowledge the issue plainly, separate what you know from what you don't, and commit to a time for the next update.
steps: Acknowledge the problem and its impact in one sentence.
Say what you know, what you don't, and what you're doing.
Commit to a specific time for the next update.
say: You're right to be concerned. Here's what we know, what we don't yet, and when you'll hear from me next.
That's on us. By Thursday noon you'll have the root cause and the recovery plan.

caseStudy.situation: After a failed system launch, a client's COO interrupted a steering committee, angry and accusing the team of hiding problems.
caseStudy.action: The programme director paused, said “You're right, the launch failed and that's on us,” listed the known facts, and promised a recovery plan by Thursday noon.
caseStudy.result: The tone shifted at once; the COO later said that call rebuilt trust.

tools.tryThis: Write a three-sentence holding statement you'd use if your current project hit a crisis today.

tools.name: Strength Plus Warmth
tools.idea: People size you up on two questions at once: can you make things happen (strength) and are you on my side (warmth)? Strength alone reads as cold; warmth alone reads as soft. Influential leaders signal both in the same conversation, often in the same sentence.
steps: Name the other person's pressure or goal first.
Then state your view clearly, without hedging.
Close with a shared next step.
say: I know your board needs a win this quarter, so I'd stop this workstream and redeploy the team.
I'm with you on the goal. I disagree on the route, and here's why.

caseStudy.situation: A new senior partner was respected for her expertise, but clients described her as intimidating and hard to approach.
caseStudy.action: Before each firm recommendation she named the client's constraint, such as “Given your hiring freeze, I'd do it this way,” and asked one personal question per meeting.
caseStudy.result: Within a quarter her client feedback moved from “sharp but distant” to “trusted adviser”.

tools.tryThis: In your next tough message, add one sentence that shows you understand their pressures.

tools.name: Full Attention
tools.idea: Charisma is mostly learnable behaviour, and its foundation is presence: complete attention on the person in front of you. People sense within seconds when your mind is elsewhere, and it quietly erodes trust. Undivided attention makes others feel important and makes you seem more powerful, not less.
steps: Put devices away and close the laptop first.
Listen to the end; pause two seconds before replying.
Sum up what you heard before giving your view.
say: Let me check I've got this: your real worry is the timeline, not the cost?
Take me through it. I'm not looking at anything else.

caseStudy.situation: A managing director noticed that junior client staff had stopped raising issues with him in meetings.
caseStudy.action: He started closing his laptop, letting silences sit, and summing up each person's point before responding: “So the risk you see is…”
caseStudy.result: Clients began bringing him problems early, and two flagged a scope risk before it became costly.

tools.tryThis: In one conversation today, check no device and sum up what they said before you answer.

tools.name: Reset Your State
tools.idea: Your inner state leaks into your body language. Anxiety shows as fidgeting, rushed speech and a higher voice, and audiences read it as low confidence. A short physical reset before high-stakes moments changes how you come across: slow breathing, relaxed shoulders, and treating nerves as readiness rather than threat.
steps: Two minutes before, take six slow breaths with long exhales.
Drop your shoulders, plant your feet, relax your hands.
Pause and make eye contact before your first word.
say: Good morning. (Pause.) I'll start with what we recommend.
Let me take a moment to answer that properly.

caseStudy.situation: A technical director dreaded board presentations; her voice sped up and she apologised for minor slide issues.
caseStudy.action: She built a two-minute reset: slow breathing in the corridor, a deliberate pause at the lectern, and a scripted first sentence she knew by heart.
caseStudy.result: Board members described her next presentation as calm and authoritative.

tools.tryThis: Before your next big meeting, take six slow breaths and script your first sentence word for word.

tools.name: Own Your Style
tools.idea: Presence is not one personality type. Quiet leaders project gravitas through clarity, preparation and well-placed silence; energetic leaders through focus and pace control. The common thread is composure, a clear point of view and reading the room. Adapt your delivery to the audience without abandoning who you are.
steps: Name your natural style: quiet, analytical, energetic or warm.
Keep its strengths; fix the one habit that undercuts you.
Ask a trusted colleague for one piece of presence feedback.
say: I'll be brief: here's my view and why.
Let me slow down here, because this is the part that matters.

caseStudy.situation: A quiet technical partner was told he lacked presence and was advised to “speak up more”.
caseStudy.action: Instead of talking more, he opened each meeting with a one-line recommendation, paused, and spoke only when he had a clear point. He kept his calm, measured style.
caseStudy.result: Clients started asking for his view first; his reserve now read as gravitas.

tools.tryThis: Ask one colleague: “What one thing would make me more convincing in meetings?”

quiz.q: You have ten minutes with a client CEO. How should you open?
options: With background on how the team got here
With your recommendation and what you need from them
With a joke to build rapport
quiz.why: Answer First: busy leaders want the conclusion first; detail can follow.

quiz.q: On a call, the client's COO says your team is hiding problems. Best first response?
options: Explain why it wasn't your team's fault
Promise it will never happen again
Acknowledge the issue, share what you know, and set a time for the next update
quiz.why: Calm Under Fire: composure and ownership build trust in a crisis.

quiz.q: A client finds you competent but intimidating. Which tool helps most?
quiz.why: You already signal strength; visible warmth makes it influential.

quiz.q: A naturally quiet leader wants more presence. Best advice?
options: Speak first and longest in every meeting
Keep their style, but lead with a clear view and use pauses
quiz.why: Own Your Style: presence comes from clarity and composure, not volume.

quiz.q: Five minutes before a board presentation, your heart is racing. What should you do?
options: Breathe slowly, relax your posture and plan your first sentence
quiz.why: Reset Your State: a short physical reset changes how calm you appear.

bite.scenario: Mid-update in a steering committee, the client's COO cuts in: “This programme is three weeks late and I'm hearing different stories from your team.” The CEO is watching. Write exactly what you say in the next 30 seconds.

bite.title: Walk in with more options than they expect
bite.framework: The Needs–Walk-away–Opening prep: six tools to uncover what both sides need, strengthen your fallback, and open with an ask you can justify. The first three prepare you; the last three work in the room.

tools.name: Find the Why
tools.idea: Positions are what people demand; interests are why they want it. Deals stall when both sides argue positions and move when someone uncovers the interests underneath. One interest can often be met in several ways, which opens options neither side had considered. Your first job is to find the need behind the number.
steps: Write down their stated position.
List three interests that might sit behind it.
Ask open questions to find out which interest is real.
say: Help me understand what's driving the freeze this year.
What would need to be true for this to work for you?

caseStudy.situation: An engineering manager's VP said “no new headcount” when she asked for two more engineers.
caseStudy.action: She asked, “What's behind the freeze?” and learned the issue was this quarter's operating margin. She proposed two six-month contractors funded from an unused software budget.
caseStudy.result: She had the extra capacity within three weeks, without adding headcount.

tools.tryThis: For your next ask, write the other side's position and three interests that could be behind it.

tools.name: Strengthen Your Walk-away
tools.idea: Your real power in a negotiation is your best alternative if talks fail. The stronger it is, the less you need this particular deal, and the other side senses it. Improve your alternative before you negotiate, set a walk-away point, and never accept a deal worse than that alternative.
steps: Write your best alternative if there's no deal.
Take one action to make it stronger before you meet.
Set your walk-away point in writing.
say: I'd like to make this work here. I'm also weighing other options.
If we can't get there, I'll understand, and I'll need to consider alternatives.

caseStudy.situation: A senior engineer wanted a promotion but felt she had no leverage with her manager.
caseStudy.action: She explored an internal transfer and had an informal chat with another team lead, then went into her review calm, knowing she had a real option.
caseStudy.result: Her manager matched the scope she wanted and fast-tracked her promotion case.

tools.tryThis: Write your walk-away in one sentence, plus one action that would make it stronger this month.

tools.name: Trade Across Issues
tools.idea: Single-issue negotiations become a tug-of-war: whatever one side gains, the other loses. Putting several issues on the table lets you trade, giving on what matters little to you and gaining on what matters most. This creates value for both sides before anyone has to split it.
steps: List every issue that could be negotiated.
Rank each by how much it matters to you, and guess for them.
Propose packages, not single concessions.
say: If base salary is fixed, can we look at title, review date and learning budget together?
I can be flexible on the start date if we can agree on scope.

caseStudy.situation: A product manager was offered a promotion with no pay increase because of budget limits.
caseStudy.action: She proposed a package: the title now, a written pay review in six months, a conference budget, and leading the new AI product.
caseStudy.result: She got three of the four, and the pay rise came at the six-month review.

tools.tryThis: List five issues you could negotiate, ranked by how much each matters to you.

tools.name: Aim High, With Reasons
tools.idea: People with specific, ambitious targets consistently get better outcomes than those who aim to “do well”. The key is justification: anchor your target in a standard the other side respects, such as market data, scope or results. A high goal without reasons feels greedy; with reasons it feels fair.
steps: Set a specific target above your minimum.
Find one external standard that supports it.
Prepare the one-sentence rationale you'll say aloud.
say: Based on the market range for this role and the two teams I now lead, I'm asking for this level.
This is in line with what comparable roles pay in our industry.

caseStudy.situation: A data lead planned to ask for “whatever is fair” in her promotion conversation.
caseStudy.action: She researched salary surveys, listed the scope she had taken on, and asked for a figure at the top of the band: “Because I now own both pipelines, I'm asking for this.”
caseStudy.result: She got 90% of her ask, well above what she would have accepted.

tools.tryThis: Find one external benchmark, such as a salary survey or comparable role, that supports your target.

tools.name: Anchor or Ask
tools.idea: The first number on the table pulls the outcome toward it. When you know the value well, make the first offer and explain it. When you don't, ask questions first and don't let their number set the range. If they anchor first and low, don't counter straight away; question the basis.
steps: Decide: am I well informed? If yes, open first.
If they open first, ask how the number was set.
Restate your justified range before you counter.
say: Can you walk me through how you arrived at that figure?
Before we talk numbers, I'd like to understand how the band was set.

caseStudy.situation: A newly promoted manager received an offer from HR well below his research.
caseStudy.action: Instead of countering, he asked, “How was this figure set?”, learned it was based on his old grade, and shared the market data for the new role.
caseStudy.result: HR raised the offer by 14% in the same call.

tools.tryThis: Draft your opening number and the single sentence that justifies it.

tools.name: Make Yes Easy
tools.idea: Your counterpart usually has to sell the deal to someone else: their boss, HR or finance. Help them by framing your proposal around their interests and giving them a simple story to tell. Proposals that make the other person look good get approved faster.
steps: Ask who else has to approve the deal.
Frame your proposal around their goals and constraints.
Offer a short written summary they can forward.
say: What will you need to take this to finance?
I'll send you a one-page summary you can share with HR.

caseStudy.situation: A team lead's director supported her promotion but warned that HR would push back.
caseStudy.action: She wrote a one-page case linking her promotion to retention risk and the team's delivery results, and gave it to her director to forward.
caseStudy.result: HR approved the promotion in the next cycle with no changes.

tools.tryThis: Ask the person you're negotiating with what they'll need to get approval.

quiz.q: Your director says, “There's no budget for a raise this year.” Which reply uses Find the Why?
options: Accept it and ask again next year
“Help me understand what's driving the budget limit this year.”
Mention you've had an outside offer
quiz.why: “No budget” is a position. Asking about the constraint uncovers interests you can work with.

quiz.q: What most increases your leverage before a negotiation starts?
options: Strengthening your best alternative if there's no deal
Preparing a longer list of demands
quiz.why: The better your fallback, the less you need this deal, and the other side can sense it.

quiz.q: The salary is fixed. Which tool helps most?
quiz.why: Bringing in title, timing and budget creates room to trade when one issue is stuck.

quiz.q: HR opens with a figure well below your research. Best first move?
options: Counter at once with a higher number
Ask how the figure was set
quiz.why: Anchor or Ask: questioning the basis stops their number setting the range.

quiz.q: Your manager supports you but has to convince HR. What should you do?
options: Give your manager a one-page case framed around the company's goals
Ask colleagues to lobby for you
quiz.why: Make Yes Easy: give your champion a simple story to sell.

bite.scenario: Your manager tells you the promotion you expected is delayed six months because of a hiring freeze, although you have led a second team since spring. You meet tomorrow for 15 minutes. Write the opening two or three sentences you will say.

exampleGrade.answer: I understand the freeze isn't your call. Since April I've run both the platform and data teams and cut release time by 30%. If the title has to wait, can we agree today on the scope, a written date and an interim pay adjustment?
exampleGrade.feedback: Strong opening. You acknowledged their constraint, anchored on concrete results and put several issues on the table instead of one demand. To make it stronger, ask one question about their interests before proposing, so your offer fits what they actually need.
exampleGrade.strength: Bundled title, timing and pay instead of a single demand.
exampleGrade.improve: Before proposing, ask: “What would need to be true to do this sooner?”
exampleGrade.modelAnswer: I understand the freeze isn't your call. Since April I've led both teams and cut release time by 30%. What would need to be true to move this before six months? If the title can't wait, could we agree today on the scope, a written review date and an interim adjustment?
